citations.quote: The toolkit's core module is QuSAD (SQL-Based CubeSat Analyse and Design Tool). It consists of an SQL and a MATLAB segment. An SQL database with available commercial off the shelf (COTS) CubeSat components was developed, currently containing more than 230 components sorted by attitude determination and control system (ADCS), electronic power system (EPS), on-board data handling (OBDH), communication, propulsion, structure, payload subsystems, and available kits.

The MATLAB segment provides a graphical user interface and an extendable modular structure that can connect and interact with the database, accommodate basic tools to assist the design process, analyse trade-off parameters, and evaluate design budgets. The user can interactively select his satellite mission using COTS components from the database and integrate them into a virtual satellite. Subsequently, the design can be analysed, saved, and optimised using the Profile Viewer to assess mass, volume, cost, link, and power budgets.

P1. An easily maintainable component database shall be established which can continuously be added with new elements. This ensures that the database can be kept updated with new component releases. The database shall be structured on subsystem level.

P2. The software shall consist of an interface to the database and be able to access the components for the CubeSat design and shall be programmed in MatLab with a modular code-build to allow further modifications and module implementations. The software shall provide a GUI for user interactions and report generation. P3. The software shall provide trade off analyses methods in the terms of design budgets with respect to major system drivers. Based on the budgets, possibilities for design optimization should be provided.

Therefore, the design concept introduced before was used as a simple guideline for QuSad's development and was further enhanced with additional design evaluation and budget analysing tools (Figure 1).

citations.quote: The power budget will calculate the generated power by solar panels and the demanded power of the consumers based on the selected components from the database. In case too much power is consumed than generated the user may have to adapt the operational scenario (reduce the on-time of components or reconsider the mission orbit). Another change to the satellite design would be to switch to more efficient solar panels or less power consuming components.

QuSAD consists of an SQL-database which is easily usable and maintainable and provides interfaces to other software. The database can only be accessed by a qualified editor via password and is structured that the database tables contain vendors and COTS components broke down and sorted on subsystem level.

The CubeSat Design module is the main section of the software consisting of several MatLab GUIs which provide user interfaces to create CubeSats (or so-called 'profiles') based on available database components. This enables the user to create and save numerous profiles with individual specifications such as name and comments. After creating a profile, the user can decide between the scientific and practice operation mode. Choosing the scientific mode will grant the software access to the SQL-database with actual COTS components while the practice mode will grant access to individually defined educational.
The user can choose and add components with the help of a Design Assistant Tool by applying a filter based on desired parameter properties to ease the decision-making process and build up a profile.

Additionally, the Profile Viewer provides the option of exporting profiles with the containing components and the entire corresponding component information's such as pictures, datasheets. This feature is especially useful to pass on a profile to a third person who is not in possession of the whole QuSAD software-package. In this case, it is sufficient to forward the file that was created after the exporting process, containing the profile data and the profile viewer GUI. The viewer provides additional interfaces to call the built-in analyse tools (see 3.3.1 ff.) to evaluate the current design.

Power budget provides an overview of the satellite's power generation and consumption. To estimate a power budget the overall average power consumption of the satellite's components during an orbit is compared to the overall average orbit power generation (OAC) of the main power sources (typically solar panels for CubeSat). A positive power margin indicates that more power is generated than consumed during an orbit. On the other hand, a negative value indicated that more power is consumed than generated during an orbit.

Using these scenarios the power generation of each scenario is calculated and weighted with the corresponding relative occurrence probability $ p_{i} $ of each scenario with overall 26 illumination possibilities. As example the probability that 2 side panels are illuminated at the same time is $ \frac{4}{26} $ . All probabilities are listed in Table 2. The adjusted powers are summed up to obtain the average power generation capability that is possible by the solar panel combination of the given CubeSat design. Based on mission duration, the end of life power generation is calculated by taking a 3% solar cell efficiency degradation per year [1] into account.

The power budget process used by QuSAD requires the orbit altitude (h) of the S/C and beta-angle ( $ \beta $ ) defined as angle between the vector to the sun and the orbital plane of the S/C. The orbit characteristics are calculated according to (3.4)-(3.7).

The battery capacity requirement during an eclipse can be calculated based on eclipse duration (as a fraction of the orbit duration), the power consumption during this time and the battery transmission (90%). The overall demanded power is a sum of the required battery capacity and the power consumption during sunlight. Based on the illumination scenarios the power generation capability is estimated and a linear degradation model of 3% per year for end of life (EOL) power generation is assumed. The overall generated power is weighted with the duration of sunlight per orbit and finally the average power margin is calculated.

To show the results the tool can generate, an example mission is defined. A 1.5 unit CubeSat for Earth observation should be designed. The satellite will be deployed from ISS in an orbit of 400 km and build with available components of the QuSAD database (Figure 6). For this example mission, the initial budget will not be limited.

After creating a "Profile" that stores all selected components the selection starts with choosing a 1.5 U structure and the other subsystems. For QuSAT LeoEye an EPS, 4 side and 2 top/bottom solar panels, S-Band/UHF/VHF antennas and transceiver, attitude control system with 3 small reaction wheels, an onboard computer and a camera payload are selected. The selected components for each subsystem is shown in the Profile in Figure 5. With the profile data, the analyses functions can be used.

The power analyses tool is able to acquire the mounted components from the profile viewer. Based on provided orbit parameters, the orbit period along with the sun and eclipse durations are calculated. This gives a baseline operational scenario for the consumers.

In the first scenario, all components (including payload) are operated in 100% of the orbit time except for the transmitter which is by default set to 10% - this approximatley equals one ground station contact. In this scenario, the selected solar panels are capable of generating a orbit average power of 3.88 Wh while the consumers require 4.79 Wh. This leads to a negative power margin of -0.905 Wh, so a design or operational scenario adoption should be considered.

The mass and volume trade-off uses the available volume and mass constraints given by the 1.5 U structure. For the cost trade-off the overall price of the components (~75892 €) is used because no limit was preliminary defined. In Figure 9 the mass budget GUI is shown. It can be clearly seen that the selected components are not exceeding the mass constraints of the structure derived from the CubeSat design specification [4], in fact, there is a margin of approx. 700 g $ \cong $ 35% of the maximum mass available. This can lead to rather considering a structure of 1 U that allows 1.33 kg and could fit the components of the current design in terms of 1.295 kg mass. A similar assessment can be made for the volume. For this budget the margin of 10 % does not allow the reduction of the structural component (see Figure 10).

To provide additional functions beyond the design phase, a battery degradation model can be implemented and to support satellite operations, the tool can be extended to be used for telemetry trending and analyses.

The presented tool QuSAD offers a dynamic, simple and intuitive software with an intuitive user interface to simplify and ease the process of satellite design for experienced space mission designers as well as for unexperienced students. Based on an SQL database, the software assists the user during the design process of CubeSat and as provides various components as well as budget analysing tools. Commercial of the shelf CubeSat components can be selected from a database to create different satellite concepts and perform initial trade-off studies. To do so, QuSAD provides price, mass, volume, link as well as power budget tools to illustrate the corresponding distributions and margins on subsystem level and to allow system design parameter trade-off studies. For maintenance of the database, it can be simply updated with new components based on MYSQL. The modular concept of the tool makes it easily extendable.

New features, like design optimization, orbit propagation, and SSA analyses module, are under development. Those upcoming upgrades will take more relevant design parameters into account and addresses the import topic of space situational awareness especially for small satellite developments and will turn the tool into S/C simulation, analyses and design tool that can be also used during satellite operations and post-mission disposal.

To keep a tool at hand that condenses the necessary knowledge of components, system, mission design, operations, and analysis functionality, the Institute of Space Systems at TU Braunschweig (IRAS) is developing an Interactive, Space Mission Analysis, Design, and Simulation Toolkit.
